launchd-plist-reload-required.body:
`launchctl kickstart -k` restarts the process but does NOT re-read the plist from disk — launchd uses its in-memory loaded config. If the plist file was edited (e.g. removing --reload), the change is invisible until the service is fully unloaded and reloaded.

**Why:** Discovered when --reload persisted in the running process after plist was fixed on disk.

**How to apply:** After editing a plist file, always do `launchctl bootout gui/$(id -u)/<label> && launchctl bootstrap gui/$(id -u) ~/Library/LaunchAgents/<label>.plist` to apply the new config. deploy.sh's `launchctl kickstart` is only correct when the plist hasn't changed.
launchd-plist-reload-required.name: launchd-plist-reload-required
launchd-plist-reload-required.tags: launchd plist kickstart bootout bootstrap reload uvicorn deploy server restart

logs-read-tool.body: Always use the logs__read MCP tool to read hook logs (domain classification, memory retrieval, tool hints, session injection). All hook events write to claude_hooks.sqlite in iCloud via sqlite_log_handler.py. Never query the DB directly with sqlite3.
logs-read-tool.name: logs-read-tool

manual-live-file-surgery-can-leave-stale.body:
After manually stopping a server, swapping/replacing a file it has open (e.g. `mv`/`os.replace` on a SQLite DB), and restarting — don't assume the very next restart is fully clean, even once the equivalent logic is later wired into proper startup code. During today's checkpoint-DB compaction work (task:5afd1b61/b623ea48), a manual live swap (stop server → checkpoint WAL → backup → compact → swap → restart) was later followed by code-driven restarts via `_compact_checkpoint_db()` in `lifespan()` — and one of those subsequent restarts still produced `attempt to write a readonly database` from `get_current_session()`, resolved only by one more explicit clean restart (`launchctl kickstart -k`) and a live verification call.

**Why:** The exact mechanism wasn't fully diagnosed (plausible theory: a persistent connection or cached file handle from the manual-surgery era lingered across an otherwise-successful restart), but the fix was simple and the failure was caught immediately — specifically because task:117e44a4's earlier timing/exception logging was already in place. Without it, this would have silently degraded again with zero signal, the same failure mode as the original 10s+ hang.

**How to apply:** After any manual intervention on a file backing a live process's persistent connection, verify with an actual functional call after the next restart (not just a health-check ping) before considering the intervention complete — especially when overlapping manual and code-driven fixes happen in the same session.
manual-live-file-surgery-can-leave-stale.name: manual-live-file-surgery-can-leave-stale-connection-state
manual-live-file-surgery-can-leave-stale.tags: stale connection, readonly database, manual db surgery, checkpoint, restart verification, sqlite

mcp-dispatch-is-table-driven-domain-map.body:
src/dispatcher.py registers MCP tools via a single DOMAIN_MAP dict: `{domain: (module_path, [action1, action2, ...])}`, and build_dispatcher() dynamically looks up `handle_<action>` on the module for each action, naming the tool `domain__action`. Removing an entire tool domain (e.g. prompt_cache__lookup/store/list/search/delete) is a ONE-LINE DOMAIN_MAP delete, not N separate handler-removal steps.

Why: task:f65bd34a's original checklist assumed 5 separate MCP tool registrations needed removing; the actual registration is table-driven, so the fix was a single dict-entry delete.

How to apply: when planning removal of an MCP tool domain in this repo, check src/dispatcher.py's DOMAIN_MAP first — the checklist item is almost always "delete the DOMAIN_MAP entry," not a per-handler enumeration.
mcp-dispatch-is-table-driven-domain-map.name: mcp-dispatch-is-table-driven-domain-map
mcp-dispatch-is-table-driven-domain-map.tags: mcp, dispatcher, domain map, tool registration, src/dispatcher.py, claude-hooks, task:e8c2646b

mcp-hook-bridge-convention.body:
MCP tools signal hook injection via a `__hook__` key in their response. `McpHookBridgeNode` pipes it to `pending_hook_output`. Zero claude-hooks code changes needed per new integration.

**Why:** Named-tool routing in _post_tool_route violates open/closed — every new MCP project requires a claude-hooks code change. Content-based routing on `__hook__` makes claude-hooks pure infrastructure.

**How to apply:** In any MCP tool response, return `{"__hook__": {"additionalSystemPrompt": "..."}}`. The bridge fires automatically. Named lifecycle tools (tasks__*) still take priority in routing — __hook__ check is the fallback.
mcp-hook-bridge-convention.name: mcp-hook-bridge-convention
mcp-hook-bridge-convention.tags: mcp hook bridge generic posttooluse additionalSystemPrompt injection open-closed factory pattern task:e766dad2

mcp-hook-bridge-is-one-way.body:
The `__hook__` convention (langchain_learning/nodes/mcp_hook_bridge.py, routed via `_post_tool_route` in session_graph.py) is a one-way channel: any MCP tool that returns `{"__hook__": {...}}` gets that payload piped straight into `pending_hook_output` → `additionalSystemPrompt` injection. It has no side-effect execution — it cannot trigger a DB write, a subprocess call, or any other stateful action.

Why: discovered while implementing commit→task-id mapping (task:a2fd402d) — considered routing MCP `git__commit` PostToolUse capture through this convention since it already exists as a generic "any MCP tool → dispatcher" bridge, but it only pipes text for prompt injection, not arbitrary logic.

How to apply: for a PostToolUse side effect (recording something, writing to a DB, calling another tool) triggered by an arbitrary MCP tool's result, add a direct function call in hooks/dispatcher.py._handle_post_tool_use (keyed on `strip_mcp_prefix(tool_name)`), not the `__hook__`/mcp_hook_bridge path. Reserve `__hook__` for cases that genuinely want to inject text into the next system prompt. See [[dispatcher-hook-event-routing]] for the broader PreToolUse/PostToolUse routing rules.
mcp-hook-bridge-is-one-way.name: mcp-hook-bridge-is-one-way
mcp-hook-bridge-is-one-way.tags: langgraph, mcp_hook_bridge, __hook__, post_tool_use, session_graph, dispatcher, side effects, additionalSystemPrompt

mcp-not-wrapping-fastapi-server.body:
Decided NOT to auto-wrap the claude-hooks FastAPI server (test worktree, port 8766) as an MCP server (e.g. via fastapi-mcp), despite the simplicity win of auto-derived tool schemas.

**Why:** the test server restarts on every `/deploy`. If MCP tool availability were tied to that same process, deploy-time restarts would drop MCP tools mid-session. Keeping the MCP layer separate/hand-rolled means it can stay up independently of hook-server deploys.

**How to apply:** keep the current hand-rolled `mcp__claude-hooks__*` tool layer as-is. Do not suggest collapsing it into the FastAPI app for "zero config" reasons — the reliability cost (coupled failure/restart domain) outweighs the maintenance savings, per user's explicit reasoning.
mcp-not-wrapping-fastapi-server.name: mcp-not-wrapping-fastapi-server
mcp-not-wrapping-fastapi-server.tags: mcp fastapi architecture decision hook server reliability deploy

mcp-tool-owns-its-hook-prompt.body:
Each MCP tool builds its own __hook__ prompt — claude-hooks is a dumb pipe. Do not let the prompt-building logic live in the hook layer.

**Why:** The tool knows its own domain context (what iteration means, what confidence means, what the user should do next). The hook layer has no business interpreting that.

**How to apply:** When adding __hook__ to a new MCP tool, write the full additionalSystemPrompt string inside the tool function itself. The bridge node never touches the content.

**Note (stale example):** `src/tools/tasks.py` no longer contains any `__hook__`/`hook_prompt` code — that file is not a current example of this pattern. The principle and the bridge node (`langchain_learning/nodes/mcp_hook_bridge.py`) are still valid; find a current __hook__-emitting tool file before citing one.
mcp-tool-owns-its-hook-prompt.name: mcp-tool-owns-its-hook-prompt
mcp-tool-owns-its-hook-prompt.tags: mcp tool hook prompt injection additionalSystemPrompt ownership responsibility separation task:1ac0c420

memory-add-batch-prefer-over-serial.body:
When adding or updating multiple memories in one operation, use `mcp__claude-hooks__memory__add_batch` instead of N serial `memory__add` calls.

**Why:** `memory__add_batch` upserts all entries in a single DB transaction and a single vector embedding call — faster, fewer round-trips, and lets the user see all changes at once before confirming.

**How to apply:**
- Any time you need to write 2+ memories (domain fixes, bulk tagging, post-task lessons) → use `memory__add_batch(memories=[...])`
- Each entry: `{"name": "slug", "type": "...", "body": "...", "domain": "...", "tags": "..."}`
- Returns `{ok, count, results: [{name, action}]}` — partial failures reported per-entry, batch continues
- Single memory with no siblings → `memory__add` is fine
memory-add-batch-prefer-over-serial.name: memory-add-batch-prefer-over-serial
memory-add-batch-prefer-over-serial.tags: memory__add_batch, memory__add, batch upsert, writing memories, multiple memories, save memories

memory-add-batch-preserve-body.body:
Never use a placeholder value (e.g. 'existing') for body in memory__add_batch when doing a field-only update. The upsert overwrites the body column — all 92 memories lost their bodies this way.

**Why:** ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE SET body=excluded.body replaces the real content with the placeholder.
**How to apply:** Before a field-only update (e.g. adding `related` or `files`), fetch each memory's current body via memory__get and pass it through unchanged. Or use a direct SQL UPDATE targeting only the new column.
memory-add-batch-preserve-body.name: memory-add-batch-preserve-body
memory-add-batch-preserve-body.tags: memory add_batch upsert body placeholder overwrite recovery loss data JSONL

memory-atomicity-audit-pattern.body:
When auditing memories for atomicity, also check for near-duplicate memories covering the same topic — they accumulate over time without being flagged as "compound" but cause injection noise. Delete the weaker one and merge unique content into the stronger one.

Also check tags for stale references (e.g., client.sh renamed to client.py) — these silently degrade BM25 retrieval without any schema violation.

**Why:** The compound-memory audit caught one staleness fix and one duplicate merge that the original checklist didn't anticipate.

**How to apply:** During any memory audit pass, run three checks: (1) compound body, (2) near-duplicate name/tags across memories, (3) stale references in tags/body that no longer match current file/tool names.
memory-atomicity-audit-pattern.name: memory-atomicity-audit-pattern
memory-atomicity-audit-pattern.tags: memory atomicity audit compound split duplicate staleness review one-fact one-file

memory-search-slug-normalization.body:
Memory search should normalize slugs before matching — strip underscores and hyphens from both the query and the slug, then compare.

**Why:** Users type slugs with underscores (claude_hooks_goals) but slugs are stored with hyphens (claude-hooks-goals), causing missed matches that waste a tool call.

**How to apply:** In `handle_search`, normalize the query and name field by replacing `_` and `-` with empty string (or a space) before LIKE comparison. Apply to the `name` column search path specifically.
memory-search-slug-normalization.name: memory-search-slug-normalization

migration-test-keep-old-ddl.body:
Migration tests must keep the pre-migration DDL inline — never replace it with the canonical (post-migration) DDL from src/db/schema.py, and never refactor it away when updating other tests in the same file to import from schema.py.

**Why:** A test named `test_migration_*` (e.g. `test_migration_backfill_from_tags` in tests/test_task_issue_type.py) exists specifically to exercise an `ALTER TABLE` backfill path. If its schema is replaced with the canonical post-migration DDL, the columns already exist before `migrate_*()` runs, so the migration becomes a no-op and the test passes vacuously without exercising anything (task:cb357eb6).

**How to apply:** Any test that deliberately creates an old schema to test an `ALTER TABLE` migration must build the DB using the old schema manually, then call the prod migrate function — leave it inline even when sibling tests get updated to import from schema.py. A comment like `# intentional: pre-migration schema` is sufficient to mark it.
migration-test-keep-old-ddl.name: migration-test-keep-old-ddl
migration-test-keep-old-ddl.tags: migration test isolation ddl schema inline pre-migration refactor preserve integrity pragma alter table task:cb357eb6

minor-followups-reuse-related-task-id.body:
For small follow-up changes to something just built (a logging tweak, a one-line fix, a tiny adjustment discovered right after closing a task), reuse the original/related task's id in the commit rather than creating a new task.

Why: user explicitly said so when asked whether to open a new task for a single added log line right after task:b9dded3e had already closed — creating a fresh task for something this small is unnecessary overhead.

How to apply: only spin up a new task when the follow-up is substantial enough to need its own Resolution/tracking (e.g. multi-step, needs grooming, spans multiple files). When a retriever imports config inside its method body (`from langchain_learning.config import config as _cfg` inside retrieve()), patching the node module's `_cfg` is not enough — the retriever re-binds `_cfg` on every call. The fixture must also patch `langchain_learning.config.config` directly.

**How to apply:** Any test fixture that redirects the memory or tool DB path must patch both the node module AND `langchain_learning.config.config` (via `patch.object(lc, 'config', cfg)`) so that late-binding imports inside retrievers see the temp DB.

multi-path-hook-prompts-stay-separate.body:
When a tool has multiple return paths (done, continue, error), write a separate __hook__ prompt per path — do not share a single builder.

**Why:** Each path has different context and different next-action instructions. Sharing a builder forces awkward conditionals and obscures intent. Three clear prompts beat one clever function.

**How to apply:** For each return json.dumps(...) block, write the hook_prompt string inline above it.

**Note (unverifiable currently):** no file in the repo currently has an active multi-path __hook__/hook_prompt implementation to check this against (the earlier tasks.py example is gone). Treat as a design principle to apply next time such a tool is built, not a confirmed-live pattern.

new-project-cwd-needs-domain-mapping.body:
Whenever a brand-new project directory is created (e.g. scaffolding a new repo for an epic, `mkdir` + `git init`), add an entry to cwd_domains.json right away — don't wait for it to come up as a problem later.

Location: `~/Library/Mobile Documents/com~apple~CloudDocs/Databases/cwd_domains.json` (iCloud-synced, path resolved via claude-hooks-dev's `src/config.py::Config.cwd_domains_json`). Format: flat `{"<directory-name>": "<domain>"}` map — usually the same string for both (e.g. `"cypress-playwright-migrator": "cypress-playwright-migrator"`).

Why: `src/tools/tasks.py::_domain_from_cwd` resolves a task's domain by walking the cwd's path components in reverse and matching against this map by EXACT component name (not substring, not full path) — see config.py's `_load_cwd_domain_map`/`cwd_domain_map`. A new project directory with no entry here means tasks__create/list calls with `cwd=<new project path>` silently fail to resolve a domain tag, which can affect task filtering/organization down the line even though task creation itself doesn't hard-fail on a missing mapping.

How to apply: as soon as a new project cwd is created (mkdir + git init, or scaffolding a sibling repo for an epic), immediately add `"<dirname>": "<domain>"` to cwd_domains.json in the same step — treat it as part of "creating the project," not a separate followup. This was done for `cypress-playwright-migrator` (epic fd7c8e12) on 2026-07-15 right after creating the directory.

Why: task:380140fa needed a field (execution_contract) that stays byte-identical every turn regardless of context pressure. The risk wasn't _enforce_context_budget (it never touches anything but memories) — it was accidentally conflating the new field with task_body's rendering path and inheriting its char-cap truncation.

How to apply: give a fixed/must-not-truncate field its own section in _format_system_prompt with no shared truncation logic, rather than appending it to an existing capped field. Write a test proving it survives both a large-memories-list budget squeeze and an oversized-body truncation scenario.

paused-epic-file-refs-go-stale.body:
When resuming a long-paused epic/task, don't trust file paths named in its body — verify them first (grep/Read), don't just act on them.

Why: epic c0f3037f (prompt-cache) was paused ~1 week, its body cited `hooks/memory_loader_lc.py` and `hooks/dispatcher.py` as the UPS pipeline location. By the time it resumed, the pipeline had been refactored into `langchain_learning/session_graph.py` — the old file survived only as a stale .pyc. Acting on the stale path directly would have wired the cache-check node into dead code.

How to apply: before implementing a task whose body names specific files/functions and which has sat open for more than a few days, spend one Explore-agent pass confirming those paths still exist and still do what the body claims, before writing code against them. Applies especially to epics/tasks resumed via /task-grooming or /what-am-i-working-on.

How to apply: when adding a node that sets pending_hook_output, check which event_type routes to it and confirm that entry point clears the field after invoke; gate rendering in hooks/dispatcher.py on hookSpecificOutput.hookEventName so cross-event payloads are never rendered.

prefer-commit-rag-over-git.body:
Always use diff_rag__smart_search before falling back to git log/show/grep when looking for code patterns, prior implementations, or commit history.

**Why:** diff_rag is semantically indexed over all commits — it finds relevant hunks by meaning, not just keywords. git commands are slower and require knowing exact strings or commit refs.

**How to apply:** Any time the task involves "find how X was done before", "look for prior implementation of Y", or "check commit history for Z" — run diff_rag__smart_search first. Only use git log/show if the RAG search returns no useful results.

protocol-as-pipe-joint.body:
Protocols in claude-hooks mark the joints in the memory injection pipe where behavioral substitution is needed:
  prompt → tokenise → MemoryRetriever → LoadMemoriesNode → additionalSystemPrompt

The three protocol joints are:
  1. MemoryRetriever — how memories are scored and fetched (langchain_learning/nodes/load_memories.py)
  2. ToolScorer     — how tool hints are ranked (langchain_learning/nodes/score_tools.py)
  3. GatePolicy     — how tool gates are dispatched (hooks/gate_check.py)

Not every node gets a Protocol — only nodes that are genuine substitution points (where a different implementation could exist and be useful).

**Why:** Mirrors LCEL Runnable | Runnable composition but in pure Python with no framework overhead. Same idea as ACME POC NodeCallable Protocol (Principle 13).

**How to apply:** When adding a new node, ask: is this a substitution point? If no, skip the Protocol. If yes, add it to retrievers.py and keep the implementation in nodes/ or hooks/.

protocol-extraction-reduces-node-code.body:
Extracting inline node logic into a Protocol-backed class consistently reduces node code by 40-60%. The node's __call__ shrinks to: extract state fields → call the Protocol method → wrap in error handling → return partial state. All SQLite, config, and scoring logic migrates to the implementation class.

**Why:** The Protocol boundary forces the question 'what is this node's job?' — the answer is always 'transform state', not 'manage DB connections'. Implementation details naturally move out.

**How to apply:** When a node has inline DB access, scoring loops, or config reads, ask if those belong in a Protocol-backed class. If yes, extract. The node gets simpler; the scorer/retriever gets testable in isolation.

pytest-addopts-silently-wins-over-bare-c.body:
A bare `pytest tests/ -q` with no explicit `-m` flag does NOT override a marker filter baked into `pyproject.toml`'s `addopts` (e.g. `addopts = "-m 'not integration' -n auto"`). Pytest merges CLI args with addopts rather than replacing them — an absent `-m` on the CLI means addopts' `-m` silently wins, with zero warning or error.

**Why:** Cost real production confidence — `scripts/deploy.sh`'s step 5 was labeled "Full suite (unit + integration)" and used a bare `pytest tests/ -q`, but every prior `/deploy` run had silently only executed the 569 unit tests, never the 63 integration tests, while reporting "passed" and shipping to main. Discovered 2026-07-05 (task:cf2f3c5f) only by noticing the test count in the "full suite" step exactly matched the dev worktree's explicit `-m "not integration"` unit-only count.

**How to apply:** Any script/doc that claims to run a "full" or "all tests" suite in a repo with an addopts marker filter must explicitly pass a marker expression that cancels it out (e.g. `-m "integration or not integration"`), never rely on a bare invocation. When auditing a CI/deploy script's test step, check `pyproject.toml`'s `[tool.pytest.ini_options].addopts` first — a suspiciously-matching test count between two "different" test runs is a strong signal one of them isn't running what it claims.

pytest-addopts-silently-wins-over-bare-c.tags: pytest, addopts, marker, integration test, deploy.sh, full suite, silent skip, CLI override

pytest-xdist-session-fixture-runs-per-wo.body:
A pytest fixture with `scope="session", autouse=True` does NOT run once per overall test invocation under pytest-xdist's `-n auto` — it runs once PER WORKER PROCESS, since each xdist worker is effectively its own independent pytest session. Code that assumes "session scope = exactly once" (e.g. a merge-in-memory-DB-to-file step at session teardown) will misbehave under xdist: multiple workers independently attempt the same one-time action, which either races or (if the action has a latent bug) makes that bug look like "always fails" rather than surfacing as an obvious intermittent race.

**Why:** `tests/test_logs.db` (claude-hooks-dev) was 0 bytes for weeks — `_merge_mem_to_file` had a real schema-init bug (assumed the target file already had a `hook_logs` table, only ever ran `ALTER TABLE` on it), masked by a bare `except Exception: pass`. Also explains why `test_parallel_faster_than_sequential` (a timing-sensitive perf assertion) only flaked when run under `-n auto`, never in isolation or without xdist — worker resource contention, not the code under test.

**How to apply:** When a "session-scoped, runs once" test fixture behaves unexpectedly under a parallel test runner (xdist, pytest-parallel, etc.), check whether it's actually running multiple times (once per worker) before debugging the fixture's own logic. More generally: never swallow exceptions bare (`except Exception: pass`) in test fixture teardown — print or log them, even in a "best effort, don't fail the test run" cleanup step, or a real bug can hide indefinitely.
pytest-xdist-session-fixture-runs-per-wo.name: pytest-xdist-session-fixture-runs-per-worker

replay-baseline-recapture-after-memory-a.body:
Replay harness deviations can be caused by adding new memories to MEMORY.sqlite during a session — new memories change scores and surface in related_tasks, causing baseline mismatches. Not always a code regression.

**Why:** The baseline is a snapshot of what the graph returns for a fixed input. New memories in the live DB change those outputs legitimately.

**How to apply:** After any session that adds multiple memories, recapture: `uv run python tests/replay_harness.py --capture`. The baseline is gitignored — it lives locally only. If deviations appear after memory additions (not after code changes), recapture is the fix, not a bug investigation.

replay-harness-also-writes-to-production.body:
CORRECTED (was factually wrong in its first version): tests/replay_harness.py does NOT write into the live server's production MemorySaver — replay_harness.py's _build_graph() constructs its own fresh MemorySaver inside its own separate OS process (`uv run python tests/replay_harness.py`), which is process-isolated from the live FastAPI server by default; no in-memory state is ever shared between them.

The REAL pollution is different: LogTaskEventsNode writes real rows into `proj_tasks.db`'s `task_events` table — a persistent SQLite file on disk, shared across processes regardless of which MemorySaver instance backs the graph. replay_harness.py's replay_event() deliberately seeds active_task_id into checkpoint state before invoking the graph (to exercise task-aware nodes like load_related_tasks/load_task_code/load_task_history), which means log_task_events sees an active task and writes a genuine task_events row with session_id='replay-<session>' — exactly what surfaced in tasks__history output during task:b63088a1's introspection.

Fix (task:a10a6638): (1) replay_harness.py's session_id now carries TEST_SESSION_PREFIX ('integration-test-replay-<session>'), (2) LogTaskEventsNode checks for that prefix and skips the task_events DB write entirely (not just the checkpoint) when present, logging a debug line instead. The prefix's job here is different from its job in task:b63088a1 — there it selects which MemorySaver a checkpoint write goes to; here it's a signal telling a DB-writing node to skip writing altogether, since replay's checkpoint isolation was never the actual problem.
replay-harness-also-writes-to-production.name: replay-harness-also-writes-to-production-checkpoint-store

retriever-top-n-none-not-hardcoded.body:
Protocol method signatures that have config-driven defaults must use `None` as the default, not a hardcoded int. Example: `retrieve(tokens, project_domain, top_n: int | None = None)` — then the implementation reads from `load_scoring_cfg()` when `top_n is None`. Hardcoding `top_n=5` silently overrode `memory_top_n=10` from src.config, causing 6 replay harness deviations.

**Why:** Replay harness caught this immediately — baseline had memories_count=10, replayed got 5. Any config-tunable limit belongs in the implementation, not the Protocol default.

**How to apply:** When extracting an inline scoring/retrieval function into a Protocol-backed class, check all numeric defaults against what the original code read from config. If it used config, the new default should be None.

retrievers-lazy-import-pattern.body:
In retrievers.py, implementation classes (CombinationSignalRetriever, KeywordOverlapScorer, DefaultGatePolicy) do all their imports inside the method body, not at module top. This is the circular-import escape hatch — retrievers.py must be importable without loading nodes/ or hooks/.

**Why:** langchain_learning.config is imported by nodes/ which also imports from retrievers.py. A module-level `from langchain_learning.config import config` in retrievers.py would create a load-time circular dependency.

**How to apply:** Any new implementation class added to retrievers.py must follow the same rule — all non-stdlib, non-typing imports go inside the method body. Protocols themselves can stay at module top (they only use typing constructs).
retrievers-lazy-import-pattern.name: retrievers-lazy-import-pattern
retrievers-lazy-import-pattern.tags: lazy import circular import retrievers protocol implementation method body load-time dependency

retrievers-py-import-safety-rule.body:
When a Protocol definition file must be import-safe, the only tolerable external import is a *type* used in a method signature. retrievers.py imports GateContext from hooks/gates.py purely for the GatePolicy.check() signature — it never calls into hooks/. The test: if you delete hooks/, does retrievers.py still compile? If yes, the dependency arrow is correct.

**Why:** nodes/ and hooks/ both import from retrievers.py. If retrievers.py imported back from either, circular imports would break at load time.

**How to apply:** Any new Protocol file in this codebase must follow the same rule — zero callable imports from the modules that will import it. Type-only imports (used only in signatures) are acceptable.

schema-py-ddl-source-of-truth.body:
src/db/schema.py is the canonical DDL owner for all SQLite tables in claude-hooks.

Tables covered: memories, open_tasks, task_events, task_edges, mcp_tool_hints, hook_logs, test_runs.
Each table has a DDL constant (MEMORIES_DDL, OPEN_TASKS_DDL, etc.) + a migrate_*_db(conn) function.

Usage:
- Tests: import DDL constants via tests/fixtures/db_factories.py factory functions
- Setup: `uv run python -m scripts.init_db` — one-time, idempotent
- Prod connect-time code (_ensure_db, _SCHEMA, etc.) NOT replaced — stays as-is

Rule: schema changes go in schema.py first. Tests get them automatically via factories.

self-updating-scripts-have-one-cycle-fix.body:
A script that updates itself via the same pipeline it runs (e.g. `deploy.sh --ship` merging a fix to `deploy.sh` itself into main) executes the OLD version of itself on the run that ships the fix — the new behavior only takes effect on the NEXT invocation, not the one currently running. Bash reads/executes the script as it existed at invocation start; there's no way for a mid-run merge to retroactively apply to the already-running process.

Why: discovered when a newly-added pre-ship divergence check in deploy.sh printed the exact noisy output a same-commit fix (`--no-merges`) was meant to suppress — the fix commit was real and correct, but `deploy.sh --ship` was still running main's pre-fix copy since the merge that installs the fix happens inside that same invocation, after the check already ran.

How to apply: don't be alarmed when a self-modifying pipeline script's own bugfix doesn't visibly take effect on the ship that lands it — verify the fix landed by grepping the updated file afterward (`grep -n "<new code>" ~/workspace/claude-hooks/scripts/deploy.sh`), not by expecting the current run's output to change. The very next invocation will use the corrected version.
self-updating-scripts-have-one-cycle-fix.name: self-updating-scripts-have-one-cycle-fix-lag

The server memory event log deliberately does NOT store assistant turns — only `prompt` (user messages) and `tool` (tool calls) events are captured.

**Why:** Removed by design — assistant turns were explicitly excluded from the event store.

server-project-root-hardcoded.body:
hooks/server.py previously had `_PROJECT_ROOT = Path.home() / 'workspace/claude-hooks'` hardcoded. This caused StaticFiles and templates to always serve from the main worktree, so CSS/template changes deployed to claude-hooks-test were invisible — the server silently served stale files from main.

**Fix applied:** All paths now live in `hooks/paths.py`. Import with `from hooks.paths import PROJECT_ROOT as _PROJECT_ROOT`. `PROJECT_ROOT` resolves via `Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent` — worktree-safe by design.

**Why:** Path.home()-based hardcode doesn't account for the git worktree model (dev/test/main are separate dirs).

**How to apply:** Never hardcode paths in server.py or any module that mounts static files. Always import from `hooks/paths.py`. Verify after deploy with `curl /ui/static/ui.css | grep <changed-rule>`.

session-id-how-to.body:
session_id is always available in the ## Turn state system prompt block (injected by the hook). Never guess it.

To look up sessions via MCP:
- Prefer mcp__claude-hooks__hooks__session_id (added task:61703ef7, 2026-07-05) — returns {session_id, turn} for the current session, no active task required, with a built-in retry that absorbs the checkpoint-write race (a brand-new session's first checkpoint write can lag a few hundred ms behind the query, which is why manually calling the session endpoint twice used to "fix" a missing session_id).
- mcp__claude-hooks__hooks__checkpoint_query previously read langgraph_checkpoints.db directly via raw sqlite3 — as of task:b3964f85 (2026-07-09) there is no longer any sqlite checkpoint file at all (see below), so this tool needs re-checking against the current codebase before trusting its description.
- curl http://127.0.0.1:8766/session returns ALL sessions (no cwd filter — that never existed despite a prior stale memory claiming otherwise), or curl http://127.0.0.1:8766/session/active for the active-task session only (returns {} if no task is active).

**SUPERSEDED (2026-07-09, task:b3964f85):** the 2026-07-05 correction below ("production uses SqliteSaver, NOT MemorySaver") is now WRONG THE OTHER WAY — production was migrated FROM SqliteSaver TO MemorySaver on 2026-07-09 after two corruption incidents (a 1.7GB bloated file, then a "database disk image is malformed" failure that silently broke Stop-hook writes). hooks/server.py's lifespan() now opens `MemorySaver()` directly — the `_CHECKPOINT_DB`/SqliteSaver code this note originally pointed to has been deleted entirely, not just superseded. See [[claude-hooks-checkpointer-migration-pending]] for full detail. Do not un-revert this back to "production uses SqliteSaver" — that was correct from 2026-07-05 to 2026-07-09 only. Verify against hooks/server.py's actual current lifespan() code, not against either historical claim in this memory.

~~Correction (2026-07-05, task:61703ef7): production uses SqliteSaver, NOT MemorySaver...~~ (kept below, struck through, for history — no longer current)

NOTE: mcp__local-mac__session__* tools (session__list_ids, session__get, session__current) have been deleted — they read the old checkpoint store, which no longer exists in that form anyway. Use hooks__session_id instead.

**Why:** session__list returned oversized payloads that caused tool result truncation. session__* tools in claude_for_mac_local were a boundary violation — removed 2026-06-23.
**How to apply:** Always read session_id from ## Turn state when visible. Use hooks__session_id for a reliable MCP-only lookup that needs no active task. Verify checkpointer choice by reading hooks/server.py's lifespan() directly each time this matters — this memory has now been wrong in both directions once each, so treat any checkpointer claim here as needing a fresh code check, not as settled fact.

When a helper function exists in a file scheduled for deletion, extract it to a shared util BEFORE writing code that depends on it — not after.

**Why:** Writing the new code first and planning to extract later risks the new code depending on a soon-deleted source, creating dead code on arrival.

**How to apply:** In grooming, check if any helper in a to-be-deleted file is needed by new code. If yes, extraction is a prerequisite checklist item, not an afterthought.

silent-skip-branches-are-ambiguous.body:
A high-frequency "fast skip" branch (fires on nearly every event/tool-call/prompt) with zero log output at ANY level is indistinguishable from that code path never running at all. This is a distinct problem from unlogged exceptions — the code isn't failing, it's just invisible, so a real regression (e.g. a routing bug that makes every call take the skip path when it shouldn't) produces the exact same silence as correct behavior.

**Why:** Audited gate_check.py, cache_check.py, activate_task.py (task:9cec0cae, 2026-07-05) and found each had at least one "nothing to do here" branch with no log call — cache_check.py logged HIT but never MISS, so a cache that silently stopped matching anything would look identical to a cache that was never being checked. hooks/gates.py, by contrast, already logged every allow/deny/fail-open path from the start and needed no changes — it's the reference example. Note: cache_check.py itself was later deleted entirely (fce7fa3, "Remove prompt-cache feature entirely") — it's cited here only as a historical example of the failure mode, not a still-existing file.

**How to apply:** When auditing a module for observability, don't just check exception handlers — check whether every meaningful branch of an if/else decision point logs its outcome, including the "took no action" branches. Use `debug` level (not `info`/`warning`) for branches that fire on every event to avoid log noise — the goal is visibility-on-demand, not a wall of INFO spam. A silent branch that fires rarely (once per session, once per error) is lower priority than one that fires on every single call.

skills-use-tools-not-implement-them.body:
Skills are prose orchestration over existing tools — they don't grow new mechanics themselves. If a skill's behavior needs a capability that doesn't exist yet, that capability gets built as a small, simple MCP tool/hook in code first; the skill then just calls it. Complexity belongs in the skill's judgment (prose), not in the tool's code — if a proposed tool is getting complex, that's a signal the design is wrong (either the tool is trying to make a judgment call that should stay in the skill, or the step should be broken into smaller, simpler tools).

A static, non-branching injection is the acceptable exception, not a violation: task:380140fa's Execution Contract (a fixed north-star string injected verbatim at task activation, same every turn, no per-turn logic) is simple code — write-once, read-verbatim — and stayed in the LangGraph/checkpoint layer rather than becoming skill prose. What made 2f0fb672's *other* pieces (per-tool Reflection, mechanical loop-detector) wrong to build in code wasn't "it's code" — it was that they required ongoing branching judgment (what changed, is this a loop, what's next) turn over turn. The dividing line is static-and-mechanical (fine as small code) vs. judgment-that-changes-with-context (belongs in skill prose or the model's own reasoning, not hardcoded).

Why: mirrors the reason 2f0fb672 was abandoned ([[behavioral-steering-lives-in-skills-not-langgraph]]) — mixing "new mechanism" work into skill prose makes the skill do two jobs (define behavior + invent plumbing), and it makes gaps hard to spot (a skill step that silently can't execute because the tool it assumes doesn't exist). Symmetrically, letting a tool grow complex to absorb judgment that belongs in the skill produces the same tangling in the other direction — brittle code standing in for prose that should have stayed prose.

How to apply: when drafting a new skill (e.g. task-implementation) or expanding an existing one, first check which steps need a tool that doesn't exist — build/extend those in code (dispatcher.py, src/tools/*.py) as their own task, then write the skill assuming the tool is already there. Keep each such tool small and mechanical (fetch, check, write one thing, or inject a fixed static string) — if implementing it starts requiring branching judgment logic that varies turn-to-turn, push that judgment back into the skill's prose instead and have the tool just expose the raw signal. Don't describe a step in skill prose that depends on a tool not yet built without flagging it as a prerequisite.

small-task-use-existing-parent.body:

**Why:** Avoids task sprawl AND hydrates the related-task graph over time. Small tasks logged under the right epic build a trail of what work has touched that area — `load_related_tasks` picks this up and gives Claude richer context in future sessions. The ancestry chain becomes the epic's memory of how it evolved.

**How to apply:**
- If the work is a single commit or a single clear action → find the most relevant open epic and use it as parent
- Use `/task-framework` or `tasks__list` to scan open epics before creating anything new
- Only create a standalone task when the work has multiple steps, a non-obvious design decision, or needs its own tracking trail

sqlite-idempotent-column-migration.body:
SQLite ALTER TABLE has no IF NOT EXISTS — adding a column that already exists raises OperationalError. Wrap each ADD COLUMN statement in try/except OperationalError for idempotent migrations.

Pattern used in src/tools/memory.py:
```python
_NEW_COLUMNS = [
    "ALTER TABLE memories ADD COLUMN last_validated TIMESTAMP",
    "ALTER TABLE memories ADD COLUMN files TEXT",
    "ALTER TABLE memories ADD COLUMN docs TEXT",
]

def _ensure_schema(con):
    for stmt in _NEW_COLUMNS:
        try:
            con.execute(stmt)
        except sqlite3.OperationalError:
            pass  # column already exists
```

Called at the top of each DB connection block in handle_add and handle_add_batch.

**Why:** SQLite doesn't support IF NOT EXISTS on ALTER TABLE (unlike CREATE TABLE). This pattern is safe to call on every connect — no-op on existing columns, applies on fresh DBs.

**How to apply:** Any time a new column is needed in an existing table, add it to _NEW_COLUMNS and call _ensure_schema(con) at the start of each connection block that writes to that table.

textual-border-box-height-auto.body:
In Textual (Python TUI framework), a widget with a fixed `height: N` (or `width: N`) combined with a `border`/`border-bottom` etc. will have the border eat into that fixed box, potentially squashing the actual content to zero size — with no exception thrown, it just silently renders blank/invisible.

Why: Textual uses a border-box model where border is drawn inside the declared box, not added outside it. `height: 1` + `border-bottom: solid` leaves 0 rows for content.

How to apply: prefer `height: auto` (or `width: auto`) whenever a widget has a border, margin, or padding and its content size isn't hardcoded elsewhere — auto-sizing correctly accounts for border+content. When a Textual layout looks broken/empty despite no errors in logs, headlessly inspect it via `app.run_test()` and check `widget.size` for each child (zero width/height is the signature of this bug) rather than assuming a logic error.

textual-screen-push-vs-refresh-in-place.body:
In a Textual app (or similar screen-stack UI), a "land on screen X" action reachable from more than one entry point must check whether the current screen is already X (refresh in place) before deciding whether to push a new instance — unconditionally pushing leaks the screen stack, so 'back'/'escape' from the new screen returns to the stale old one instead of the true previous screen.

Why: found in tui/app.py (SeniorDevAgent) — load_db()/run_pass1() always did push_screen(ListScreen()), which was fine from the single entry point during initial dev, but broke once a second entry point (switching db while already inside ListScreen) was added.

How to apply: for any navigation helper that can be invoked from multiple call sites, branch on `isinstance(self.screen, TargetScreen)` — refresh in place if already there, push fresh only if not.

tool-hints-saturation-problem.body:
High-frequency universal tools (vault__write, vault__read, session__save_summary) accumulate counts fast and will eventually dominate BM25+domain retrieval, crowding out lower-count but contextually precise tools.

**Why:** Count-weighted scoring has no ceiling — a tool used 500x scores 10x higher than one used 50x, even if the 50x tool is the right one for the prompt.

**Plan needed:** Implement a saturation cap or IDF-style normalization in ToolHintsRetriever. Options:
1. Clamp count contribution above threshold N (e.g. log(count) instead of count for ranking)
2. Flag tools as universal (domain=global + count > threshold) and exclude from scored retrieval — always inject them separately as ambient context
3. Two-tier retrieval: universal tools in a fixed header, BM25 scores only non-universal tools

**How to apply:** Revisit when any global-domain tool exceeds ~100 uses or when retrieval quality noticeably degrades (wrong tools surfacing for niche prompts).

toon-default-rollout-grep-internal-calle.body:
Before defaulting any existing MCP tool's return shape to a new format (e.g. TOON instead of JSON), grep the WHOLE repo for internal Python callers of that handler function — not just its MCP dispatcher registration.

Why: `read_logs_sqlite`'s TOON-default change (task:d2165715) was safe because it had zero internal callers. `tasks__list`'s handle_list (task:4b5bf21f) DID have 5 internal callers in `hooks/ui/routes.py` expecting the old `list[dict]` shape — missed during implementation, and the unit suite stayed green throughout (621 passed both before and after introducing the bug) because unit tests only exercise `src/tools/tasks.py` directly, never routes.py's integration with it. Only the integration suite (spinning up the real FastAPI app) caught the `AttributeError: 'str' object has no attribute 'get'` at deploy time.

How to apply: for any task that changes a shared function's return shape/contract, run `grep -rn "handle_<name>(" --include="*.py" .` across the whole repo (not just tests/ or the dispatcher) as a mandatory pre-implementation step, and update every internal caller to pass the explicit format/param it needs. Treat "the unit gate passed" as insufficient evidence for this class of change — only the integration suite (or the grep) actually proves it. See [[toon-encoding-shared-module]].

unbounded-growth-has-two-independent-dim.body:
A retention/eviction policy that caps "how many concurrent things exist" (e.g. active sessions/threads) does not automatically cap "how much history accumulates within one still-active thing" — these are independent growth dimensions, and a fix for one silently leaves the other unbounded.

**Why:** `_trim_checkpoints()` correctly capped concurrent Claude Code sessions (evicts whole inactive thread_ids) from day one, but nothing bounded how many checkpoint VERSIONS a single long-running thread accumulates — LangGraph's SqliteSaver writes one full-snapshot row per graph step and keeps every version by design (time-travel/resumability). One unusually long conversation (this session, 2026-07-05) reached 5976 checkpoint rows / 447k writes rows / 1.68GB before `get_current_session()`'s `checkpointer.list()` started hanging 10s+. The bug was invisible for a long time because it only bites the rare long-running-session case, not the common one the original cap was designed around.

**How to apply:** When designing any cap/eviction policy, explicitly ask both "how many concurrent instances am I bounding?" and "how much history within one instance am I bounding?" — don't assume capping one automatically bounds the other. Also: when adding a NOT-IN-based cleanup query (e.g. orphaned `writes` rows), prefer "delete anything not currently in the retained set" over "delete only rows tied to what I'm evicting right now" — the latter misses pre-existing orphans that predate the fix (47,652 distinct checkpoint_ids in `writes` vs only 30 in `checkpoints`, most already orphaned before this session's fix ran).

ups-context-sources-all-capped.body:
All UPS-injected system-prompt context sources are bounded, as of task:251a8531: memories (4000-token budget trim, task:3de05199), related_tasks/related_commits/task_rag_chunks (top-3 each, pre-existing), task_context (20-turn SQL LIMIT, pre-existing), mid_task_decisions (last-15 slice, task:251a8531), task_body (3000-char truncation, task:251a8531). task_context_summary (from SummarizeTaskContextNode) was dead code from 2026-06-22 through 2026-07-04, but was re-enabled in task:b9dded3e — it is now live again, gated to fire at most once per task activation (first-turn-only, via len(task_context) <= 1), so its contribution to injected context is bounded by construction (a single ≤200-word bullet summary), not by _enforce_context_budget.

Why: memories was fixed first because it was the obvious uncapped one, but an explicit audit found two more silent unbounded-growth risks (mid_task_decisions grows every tasks__add_decision call over a task's life; task_body has no length cap at all).

How to apply: if a new UPS context-producing node is added, check whether its output list/string is naturally bounded (top-N query, fixed schema) or can grow with session/task lifetime (checkpoint-appended lists, raw DB text) — the latter needs an explicit cap, don't assume it's covered by _enforce_context_budget unless you add it there. If summarize_task_context.py is ever disabled/removed again, update this memory back.

verify-dev-worktree-features-in-process-.body:
Never verify a brand-new dev-worktree feature by calling it through the live MCP tools (mcp__claude-hooks__*) before /deploy — those tools run against the persistent claude-hooks-test server process, which only picks up dev's code after a redeploy. A feature that's genuinely working in dev's source can appear broken/missing through the live tools simply because the running process is stale.

Why: after adding document.implementation to TaskDocument and wiring it into handle_update (task:4d3a6fc5), calling mcp__claude-hooks__tasks__get on the live server showed no "implementation" key at all in the document — looked like the feature silently failed. It was actually just the untouched claude-hooks-test server running pre-change code. Verified correctly instead by importing directly from the dev worktree's src/tools/tasks.py in a throwaway Python script with a patched _DB path.

Related: [[dev-gate-removal-task-close-gotcha]] is the same root cause (test server lags dev until /deploy) applied to gate removal specifically — this memory generalizes it to ANY new feature verification, not just gates blocking calls.

How to apply: to sanity-check new dev-worktree behavior before it's deployed, either (a) run the unit test suite (already does this correctly, in-process against dev), or (b) write a small standalone script that imports the dev worktree's modules directly with a patched DB path — never trust a live mcp__claude-hooks__* call as proof a just-written dev change works, until after /deploy.

verify-endpoint-params-against-code-not-.body:
A memory or docstring claiming an API endpoint accepts a specific query param (e.g. "?cwd=<path>") should be verified against the actual route handler before relying on it — an unrecognized query param to a FastAPI/Starlette route is silently ignored by default, not rejected, so a wrong claim about accepted params doesn't fail loudly; it just quietly does nothing.

Why: memory verify-session-id-via-hooks-server claimed GET /session accepted an optional ?cwd=<path> filter. The actual hooks/server.py handler takes no params at all and returns every session unfiltered. The mistake persisted because passing the bogus param never errored.

How to apply: before trusting a memory's claim about an endpoint's accepted parameters, grep the route handler's function signature directly — don't assume a memory is current just because it reads confidently.

verify-production-path-before-accepting-.body:
When grooming or implementing an infra/plumbing task, verify the task's own stated premise against actual runtime behavior (git history of the relevant file, live grep for callers, direct inspection of the running DB/service) before accepting it at face value — don't just implement what the task description says needs to happen.

Why: three tasks in one session chain each had a wrong or incomplete premise that only surfaced by checking the real production path directly, not by trusting the task body:
- task:4b5bf21f ("default tasks__list to TOON") — task didn't mention hooks/ui/routes.py's 5 internal callers; only caught by running the integration suite, not by reading the task.
- task:46634a19 ("add groomed_at to schema.py") — the task named the WRONG FILE for the actual production fix; schema.py isn't the prod path, src/tools/tasks.py's own inline _ensure_db()/_migrate() is. Caught by grepping _connect()'s call chain during grooming.
- task:9d3acbef ("consolidate schema.py/tasks.py duplication") — the task's entire premise (that the duplication was accidental drift to fix) was wrong; it's a deliberate 2026-06-27 design decision (commit de1ae61/task:cb357eb6). Investigating *why* the split existed (git log --follow, reading the original commit) surfaced a real, more serious bug instead (task_edges missing from the self-healing prod path entirely — a live crash risk, masked only by scripts/init_db.py having been run once manually).

How to apply: before implementing a task that touches "which file/module is authoritative," "does X get called from Y," or "is this the production path" — spend one grep/git-log/live-inspection step confirming the premise, even if the task body sounds confident. This is now a standing part of how grooming should treat this class of task, not a one-off. See [[toon-default-rollout-grep-internal-callers]] for the internal-callers-specific variant of this same principle.

verify-session-id-via-hooks-server.body:
When a tool call needs the current session_id (e.g. tasks__create/set_active), verify it against the hooks server rather than guessing from a project jsonl filename.

Why: guessing from the most-recently-touched .jsonl in ~/.claude/projects/<project>/ can silently pick a stale or wrong session if multiple sessions/files exist for the same project.

**Correction (2026-07-05, task:61703ef7):** GET /session takes NO query params — the `?cwd=<path>` filter this memory previously claimed does not exist in hooks/server.py's actual implementation (it just returns {"sessions": [{"session_id", "turns"}]} for every session in the live checkpointer, unfiltered). Passing ?cwd= is silently ignored, not an error, so the mistake wasn't obvious.

How to apply: prefer the new mcp__claude-hooks__hooks__session_id tool — it returns {session_id, turn} for the current session specifically, with a built-in retry that absorbs the checkpoint-write race (no active task required, unlike /session/active). Fall back to curl http://127.0.0.1:8766/session only if that tool is unavailable, and note it returns ALL sessions (no filtering) — you must disambiguate by turn count/recency yourself.

vscode-mcp-json-workspacefolder-relative.body:
claude-hooks-dev/.vscode/mcp.json registers the claude-hooks stdio MCP server using ${workspaceFolder} instead of a hardcoded path (e.g. /Users/debaditya/workspace/claude-hooks-dev).

Why: this repo is developed as a git worktree (dev branch at claude-hooks-dev, prod/main branch at claude-hooks). A hardcoded path would need editing every time the config is copied between worktrees; ${workspaceFolder} makes the same file work unmodified in both.

How to apply: when adding VS Code / Copilot MCP configs for repos that use the dev/test/main worktree pattern, always prefer ${workspaceFolder}-relative command/args over absolute paths.

worktree-diff-detects-stray-direct-edits.body:
When a multi-worktree repo (dev/test/main) is supposed to only flow one direction (dev→test→main via /deploy), an uncommitted modification found directly in main is a signal someone (human or a prior session) edited main out of band — don't just discard or commit it blindly.

Why: found via a plain `git status` in ~/workspace/claude-hooks that showed two modified skill.md files main had never had committed. Diffing against dev's committed HEAD showed main's uncommitted version was actually *newer* (already contained content dev didn't have yet) — proof the edit bypassed the pipeline rather than main simply lagging behind.

How to apply: before resolving stray uncommitted changes in a downstream worktree (test/main), diff them against the upstream worktree's HEAD to determine direction — if the downstream version is newer/more complete, port the content upstream (dev) and commit there, then discard from the downstream worktree so the pipeline invariant (only /deploy touches main) is restored, rather than committing directly to the downstream branch or discarding the only copy of new work.
